title: The Trench
hook: Salman the Persian suggests a trench, and all dig, the Prophet ﷺ among them, hungry (33:9–11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hamzah, the lion of God, and a grief that forgave. Your line was the lion fell. Did you tell someone about a brave person you remembered? Day two hundred sixty-eight.

Two years after Uhud, the news is worse than ever. Mecca has gathered allies from all over Arabia. An army of about ten thousand, the biggest anyone there has seen, is coming to finish Medina for good. The city has maybe three thousand fighters. There's no wall. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls his companions together to plan, and the ideas go around the circle. And then a man speaks up who isn't from Mecca, or from Medina, or from Arabia at all. He's a Persian, a former slave, and he says: where I come from, when we're besieged, we dig a trench. The early biographers say no one in Arabia had fought that way before. Today: the Trench.

The man was Salman al-Farisi, Salman the Persian. He had left his home in Persia as a young man searching for the truth, traveled through Syria, been sold into slavery, and ended up in Medina, where he became Muslim. The Prophet took his idea, and the whole city dug. The trench ran across the open northern side of Medina, where horsemen could charge. It was winter, and cold. Food was so short that, according to a hadith in at-Tirmidhi, men tied a stone against their stomachs to quiet the hunger, and the Prophet had tied two. Sahih al-Bukhari says he carried earth until the dust covered his belly, and chanted with the diggers as they worked. When they hit a rock no one could break, they called him, and he took the pickaxe himself and struck until it crumbled. Then the army arrived, and stopped. Horses can't jump a deep ditch. The siege dragged on for weeks. The Qur'an describes how it felt inside the city: the enemy came at you from above and below, eyes grew wild, hearts rose into throats, and the believers were shaken hard. And then, it says, God sent a wind, and hosts they could not see. A cold, violent wind tore through the enemy camp at night, overturning pots and blowing out fires, and the great army packed up and left. The Muslims remember it as the battle of the Trench, or the Confederates, al-Ahzab, the name of the surah that tells it. And they remember who had the idea.
screen: `SALMAN THE PERSIAN.` · `A STONE AGAINST THE HUNGER.` · `HEARTS ROSE INTO THROATS.` · `A WIND, AND THEY LEFT.` · then, large: `DIG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept a good idea from an outsider. Sit, and think of a problem you've been stuck on. Now think of who you haven't asked. The new person at work. Someone from a different country or generation. A kid. Someone whose way of doing things is nothing like yours. Imagine asking them, and actually listening, the way the Prophet listened to Salman. Then picture everyone digging together. The bell holds the time.
The Trench. Salman the Persian's idea, dug by the whole city, the Prophet among them, that held back an army of ten thousand. Today's word.
Your line: dig together. Today, ask one outsider for their idea, and do the work alongside the people you're with. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the battle of the Trench through Surah al-Ahzab, and Salman al-Farisi is honored as an example of a seeker from far away, embraced by the community.

myth: the trench was an old Arab way of fighting
the early biographers say it was new in Arabia, an idea Salman brought from Persia.
the Prophet dug and carried earth himself
Sahih al-Bukhari says the dust covered his belly.
the siege ended in a great battle at the trench
the Qur'an says God sent a wind and unseen hosts, and the army left.

fork.setup: you're planning to defend a city with no wall. a newcomer from far away suggests something no one here has ever done. what do you do?
options: ask him to prove it first.
fork.reveal: the Prophet took Salman's idea, and the whole city dug. the army of ten thousand couldn't cross.

original.note: Arabic: the trench, a word itself borrowed from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle story.
what it means: a city that dug a Persian idea together, hungry and cold, and was spared by a wind.
what a scholar hears: khandaq is a Persian loanword, fitting the story; Bukhari 4099–4104 give the digging, and 33:9–11 the fear inside the city.

sources.ref: Qur'an 33:9–11 (the wind and unseen hosts; eyes grew wild, hearts rose to throats)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4099–4104 (the digging, the rock, the dust)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham); al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi: Salman's suggestion; numbers

notes: Salman's suggestion is in the sirah and maghazi literature (Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi, Ibn Sa'd), not in Bukhari; confirm.
Numbers (about 10,000 confederates, about 3,000 defenders) follow the sirah; confirm.
Jabir's small meal that fed many (Bukhari 4101) is left out for length.
khandaq as a Persian loanword (from kandag): widely stated; confirm.
'No one in Arabia had fought that way' now attributed to the early biographers rather than stated flat; confirm.
The dust covering his belly may be Bukhari 4104 or 4106; the cited range 4099–4104 is from memory, check the number.
Banu Qurayzah's role and its aftermath are left out; a Keeper should decide how and where the path handles that history.
